Title: spin-off topic: Is deal making inherent to mutiplayer games?

Messages.Author: Teeka
Messages.Body:
-- (Thought I'd better make a new thread, since it's not really adding
to the discussion about deal-making in tourneys, but I did want to
share this with everyone.) ---

Both Josh and LSJ have said it, and the whole deal making-discussion
is based on it being true: "deal making/table talk is inherent to
VTES, because it's a multiplayer game."

I disagree with this. I don't see why deal making/table talk would
have to be part of VTES, or any multi-player game. It can be, easily,
of course, but it can just as easily not be. I'll try to explain what
I mean.

First of all, as someone already stated, deal making is not covered in
the rules. Basically this means that it's not an inherent part of the
game, but it's not disallowed either. To me, this in turn means that
it's all up to the players to do or not do it. Just like dressing in
all-blue clothes or playing while hanging upside down.

I have played many, many multiplayer games over the years. Games like
Settlers of Catan, or Risk, or Magic with more than two players (which
is the way I always play it) to name but a few.
All of these games could, possibly, have a strong level of deal
making: "I'll trade you the ore you need if you promise not to block
my trade route" (Catan), "I'll counter that Terror if you promise to
play that +2/+2 enchantment on my creature" (Magic). Without a doubt,
this is the way some people play those games.
But still, never ever have I, or anyone I played with, felt the need
to make deals. We all felt that such behaviour would be something
additional, added by the players themselves, which we don't want, we
want to play the game *as it is*. Frankly, it never even really
occurred to me as an option. If it's not in the rules, then it's not
in the game.

When I want to play VTES, I want to use the *cards*. I want to use the
strategies made possible by the *cards* and win because I am good with
the *cards*. I like how lots of aspects of this particular game
invlove dealing with multiple other players, I especially like how
referendums work and the "eligible-to-block"-rules.
However, I want the interaction-factor to be limited by what the
*cards* can do. Meaning: I could spare a player by not damaging him
with my KRC, but I'd have no idea if he'd return the favor. I would
never discuss it, only give out a signal by doing something benevolent
and hope for help later, which might prove to be a mistake. I could
rescue my grandpredator's vampire from torpor hoping that that vampire
will be used to block and kill my predator's vampire. But I won't
offer to do it in return for a promise for help later on. I think the
workings of a card like Bribes is in-game deal making (made possible
by a card) which is fine.

So I'm actually playing SoD in every mutiplayer game I play, without
seeing it as a "special format". Quite the contrary, I see it as the
"normal" way to play a game.
If I wanted to do something in my spare time that involved lots of
debate, I'd become a board member for some union. Instead, I spend my
money on cards and my time on making decks, so I want to *play those
cards*, not play only a few of them and let the rest of the game
depend on how well I can talk.

I think deal making and table talk reduce the value of the cards and
strategies made available to us by R. Garfield, LSJ and everyone else
that's designed (parts of) VTES. What's the use of having hundreds of
cards and many card-based strategies, if deal-making is just as
important, if not more so, to get you the VPs/wins?
To me, deal making can (if not does) reduce the cards themselves to a
second-rate aspect of the game, merely a way to establish a strong
position in the inevitable verbal power struggle.

Having said all this, I want to point out I fully understand that
things have evolved the way they have and this is the way lots of
people like it. I totally see all the arguments why deal making can be
allowed and not saying they're wrong. I just differ in opinion on the
whole assumption that it *has* to be part of VTES.

-Teeka, who would certainly get a time-wasting warning beacuse he can
never explain himself in just a few words. :-)

Because R. Garfield designed the game to be that way, and the cards are designed

The text of Succubus Club even holds indications of that.

It doesn't have to be, of course, as evidenced by the Silence of Death format.

It just happens that V:TES was designed with it as a part. (And note that the
evolution direction is the other way -- V:TES started with deal-making included
and the Silence of Death format was created later).

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Jun 21, 11:57 am, Teeka <teeka_dra...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> Both Josh and LSJ have said it, and the whole deal making-discussion
> is based on it being true: "deal making/table talk is inherent to
> VTES, because it's a multiplayer game."

Clearly, I pretty much agree with you. As a multi player game, a
certain level of negotiation is unavoidable, really. But how much of
that happens is dependant on the whim and desire of the players. When
it becomes a problem is when the whim of some players to negotiate
starts to infringe on the whim of other players to play the part of
the game that is not involiving negotiating.

As noted, the rules for VTES in no way recognize dealmaking and
negotiating. The tournament rules do, but primarily in reference to
*limiting* dealmaking and negotiating, rather than mandating or
encouraging them.

Some folks *really* like deal making/bargaining/negotiating in their
games of VTES. Which is fine. Until it makes it hard for other people
who do not have the same wishes to play the game that they want to
play. Granted, there are a lot of situations where what player A
thinks is fun is going to infringe on what player B thinks is fun, for
example:

- Player B likes 4CL and player A does not.
- Player A likes rush combat and Player B hates having his vampires
beat up.
- Player A likes arbitrarily back ousting and ignoring his own victory
conditions, and Player B thinks this is stupid.

But because this is a game, in instances where players like different
things, what is actually supported by the rules wins out. At least in
my mind. In the first example, yeah, player B like 4CL, but the rules
support Player A, so player B has to suck it up or do something else.
In the second example, getting yor vampires beat up is a large part of
the game by design, so player B has to suck it up, adapt, or do
something else. In the third example, Player B is supported by the
tournament rules that arbitrarily back ousting is stupid, as it is not
playing to win, and if you are playing in competition, you are
required to try and win.

Dealmaking and negotiation are *not* however, supported by the rules
of the game--the rule book does not even mention dealmaking and
negotiation, as far as I can tell. So while due to this being a multi
player game, yeah, a certain level of negotiation is a likely result,
it needs to be contained within reason, lest folks not involved in the
negotiation session get shortchanged, in terms of their ability to
play the game they want to play.

If everyone at the table is having a good time negotiating and
dealmaking, great. They are having fun. More power to them. But if
three people are spending a significant portion of time wheeling and
dealing, leaving the other two to sit and do nothing as the clock
ticks away, and those two object to this expenditure of time, they are
in their rights (at least in my head) to have a judge put an end to
it.

> I think deal making and table talk reduce the value of the cards and
> strategies made available to us by R. Garfield, LSJ and everyone else
> that's designed (parts of) VTES.

As far as I recall from reading Garfield's design note on the game, he
seemed to specifically *want* to design a multi player game where the
impact of negotiation was limited (see: predator/prey dynamic;
inherrent political rules). The current tournament rules also seem
specifically designed to attempt to limit the impact of negotiation
(see: PTW; Game Win rule; deals are void in end game).

-Peter

Well, I don't think I said that dealmaking is necessarily inherent to
all multiplayer games. But table talk is.

It is, IMO, unavoidable that table talk is part of every multiplayer
game unless the rules specifically prohibit it. Dealmaking is also
profitable in many multiplayer games, though the rules structure of
some makes it less useful (and therefore less common) than in others.
Then beyond that, there's the "gentleman's agreement" approach, which
is basically what you're describing, which is that people don't offer
or accept deals because "that's just not how it's done."

Which is fine in a way, but it's also no more or less reliable than
the "social pressure" method of getting people to not play stealth-
bleed decks to make a 4CL environment "balanced" in VTES.

> So I'm actually playing SoD in every mutiplayer game I play, without
> seeing it as a "special format". Quite the contrary, I see it as the
> "normal" way to play a game.

the tournament rules (if not the rulebook itself) to prohibit table-
talk and dealmaking.

> I think deal making and table talk reduce the value of the cards and
> strategies made available to us by R. Garfield, LSJ and everyone else
> that's designed (parts of) VTES. What's the use of having hundreds of

> To me, deal making can (if not does) reduce the cards themselves to a
> second-rate aspect of the game, merely a way to establish a strong
> position in the inevitable verbal power struggle.

Oh yes. It definitely does. I think it is virtually impossible to
succeed in high-level competitive VTES without being willing and able
to participate in the negotiation part of the game.

Josh

A number of the big tournaments disallow it. Several more disallow
talk of deals at the table - one fairly notable tournament this year
ended with the last two players literally walking away from the table
to make their deal arrangement, then back to playing things out per
their agreement.

And even with that limitation, yeah, a lot of poker tournaments have
deals, both in terms of how (many) pros swap 'pieces' of each other
before the tournament starts (i.e. 'we'll give each other 5% of our
earnings when we're done' or 'I'll pay half your entry fee and you
give me a quarter of your winnings') and in terms of deals made when
it's down to the last few players.

There's been a little mini-controversy at the WSOP this year, as one
prominent player offered a deal to another player, asked a tourney
director if doing so was okay and got approval, only to later find out
the director was ignorant of the actual rules - the player's response
has basically been that many, many people had such deals, and always
did, but that he was getting scolded for actually asking permission
and making his arrangement public.

> For what it's worth. I'm not sure if it has much relevance to VTES
> deal making or not. :-)
>
> Josh

-John Flournoy

On 21 jun, 18:44, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:
> Teeka wrote:
> > First of all, as someone already stated, deal making is not covered in
> > the rules. Basically this means that it's not an inherent part of the
> > game, but it's not disallowed either.
>
> That logic is flawed. If it were true that deal making is not covered, that
> still wouldn't necessarily imply that deal making is not an inherent part of the
> game.
>

Don't think so. I'd say that a rulebook should cover all there is to
say about the game itself, apart from what anyone would decide to do
with them, or add to them later.
The rulebook and the texts on all the cards are what embody *the game*
as an entity. Even though many people add things to it, (like table
talk and deals, or a card limit, or having pizza whether you want to
or not) those things are not an inherent part of the game itself, but
an inherent part of the way it *turns out to be played by a number of
people*, which is something different. If the majority of players
decided to always play with their underpants on their heads, that
would become an inherent part of the game *as played*, but unless
there's rules about it, not a part of the game itself.

> Also, deal making is covered in the V:EKN rules.

I know. But just the tournament rules. Not the actual rulebook (still
two different things, right?). And lots of those VEKN rules exist
because people started adding non-inherent things (that weren't
covered by the rules), and those things had to be contained. Not the
other way around. If people would stick to doing things that are made
possible by the rules and card texts and nothing else, many of the
VEKN rules would not be necessary but the game could still be played
perfectly fine.

> Just because deal-making isn't mandatory doesn't mean it isn't a part.
>
> If you and your friends never feel the need to use bleed bounce, that doesn't
> mean bleed bounce isn't part of the game *as it is*.
>

Dare I say it?.... ....yes I do. That analogy is flawed. ;-)
Bleed bounce IS an inherent part of the game, because it is made
possible by the text on certain cards. Deal-making through table talk
is not made possible by any card text or rule in the rulebook. It is
added by people. It's not a matter of what I personally would like, or
feel the need to use, at all, that's my whole point.

> Because R. Garfield designed the game to be that way, and the cards are designed
> the cards under that framework.
>
> The text of Succubus Club even holds indications of that.
>

I'd say the text of SC indicates that he intended for *certain* deals
to be possible only through use of a specific card, which I say is
fine. Golden rule, cards overrule the rulebook. Plus, designing a card
that makes something possible would, I think, prove that he intended
that something to not be possible otherwise. Why else design SC? I
mean, if he intended or expected all VTES players to speak in rhyme,
there'd be no Madness Ot Bard either. He didn't, so he made a card
that made it mandatory. Dumb card, I know, but you get the point.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <1182441454....@g4g2000hsf.googlegroups.com>, Teeka

<teeka_...@hotmail.com> writes:
>I have played many, many multiplayer games over the years. Games like
>Settlers of Catan, or Risk, or Magic with more than two players (which
>is the way I always play it) to name but a few.

>All of these games could, possibly, have a strong level of deal
>making: "I'll trade you the ore you need if you promise not to block

>my trade route" (Catan), "I'll counter that Terror if you promise to

>play that +2/+2 enchantment on my creature" (Magic). Without a doubt,
>this is the way some people play those games.
>But still, never ever have I, or anyone I played with, felt the need
>to make deals.

Lots of people do, in all sorts of such games. It very much depends on
who you play with. Some people have a culture, spoken or unspoken, of
"fight the good fight" and will only try to win under their own steam.
Others will co-operate to get wins. Others will wheel and deal and
scheme and plot in order to pull a win out of their ass when everything
looked awful. Those in different categories will regard other people in
other categories in different ways - someone who uses whatever legal
tactics they can to win will often regard someone who refuses to
backstab or deal extensively as honourable but easy to manipulate or
predict, or whatever.

What can make a significant difference, however, is the structure of the
game.

1) Is there any prize of any worth, or are we playing for
pride/fun/something fairly trivial?
2) Is there a defined, or easily derived, second place?

As others have pointed out, poker can get many, many deals - because you
have a huge pot of money to split. If you're only ever playing for fun,
or the prize is that you get the extra slice of pizza, it's going to be
much harder to split things with people. OF course, if you play
sometimes for fun but sometimes for a huge prize, the fun games may
become more competitive as people practise.

However, you can also find games pan out quite differently if someone
can take a second place - particularly if that means something, like
qualifying for a spot on the final table.

If the *only* thing that mattered in V:TES was getting Table Wins, you'd
see a hell of a lot less VP dealing. (This would also cause many
problems in smaller tournaments, where you wouldn't get enough players
for the final, and have a number of other unpleasant side effects.) It
doesn't matter to me if you get a 3-2 split or a 5-0 split, if I'm the
one on the losing end. The 2VP don't count for anything, except
possibly pride. Whereas if I'm in a position where those 2VP are
valuable to me (higher rank, final table seat, qualifying for a
continental championship), I will want them.

Were you to want to minimize deal-making in V:TES, you would probably
need to find some method of:

- incentivising TW over VP, even more than now
- making a sweep significantly better than a 3-2 split (say, a sweep
counted for 2 table wins, so I'm less likely to make rollover
deals or withdraw deals)
- maintaining a way of tie-breaking, so that the small 10 player
tournament with two tables where only 2 different players get
Game Wins, but try to minimize the reward (this is very, very,
very hard - some players just will play for that tie-breaker,
almost no matter what you do, unless there's a random choice of
tie-breakers, and that would suck a bit)
- potentially, making timeouts a problem for all players on the table,
so that speedy play is encouraged (say, all players get -0.5VP,
not +0.5VP) and lengthy table talk discouraged, without actually
preventing it where necessary
- tying this all together so that players can't game the system ("hey,
if we timeout, Billy Bob will lose the 0.5VP that would keep him
on the final table..."), at least in any egregiously distasteful
fashion
- possibly, trying to prevent "spoilers" or sort of king-making -
players whose only incentive is to disrupt the table in such a
way as to prevent the winner getting the extra benefits (e.g. in
my sweep = 2TW example, you might prevent a sweep by letting
yourself be ousted, because it makes no difference to you who
ousts you, and you're feeling mean).

Note that none of this is easy. Also the example tweaks, such as making
a sweep worth 2TW, are just random examples off the top of my head
(having seen similar-ish things suggested in the past, though), rather
than serious, considered suggestions.

Note that even then, you could easily see table splits on the final
table at a tournament with a decent prize, where I offer you half of the
box of boosters for your help.

This is a strawman.

First, hello, it's a CCG. The business model doesn't work like that.
Second, no two players playing the same deck ever play it in the same
way - some players are better than others, some players are better with
specific decks than others (some aren't good at combat, say, whereas
others are just great with it). Skill at playing the non-deal-making
part of the game is no small part of actually winning.

Note also that in an environment where you find that deals are causing
you too much trouble, you may find that learning to spoil deals
effectively is in your interests, and will work in your favour. This
does not have to be dealing with other people. It can be removing a
player from the table who, otherwise, you would have left alone. Judge
comes over and examines playing to win: "Well, if I leave him on the
table, the two of them are going to oust me. That can be playing to
win. In the situation I'm in, I'm choosing to remove him, because I can
choose how I die, so I chose this way. And if it stops me dying, that's
good for me too."

This isn't very hard, but is overlooked too often. Players do not make
deals out of diamond. They can be affected. Their deals can be
affected, nullified, or simply quashed. Maybe you wouldn't normally
cross-table rush and dunk Anneke in a situation like this, but now that
Anneke has offered her support to help your predator oust you (passing
his KRCs, burning you in bloodhunts, blocking you now and then,
whatever), you cross-table rush her and dunk her. Or you Kindred
Spirits bleed her. Or she gets Pentex Subversion, not your prey.

Disrupt the deals. Threaten to disrupt them when they're being made.

bounce, but it might be advantageous to you. Or not.

>the
>existing ones *imposing* deals as part of the game.

play decks that bleed for 13 is being imposed.

Base your interpretation on the reasonableness of the player's
decisions. It's reasonable for her to assume the deal will be honored

You say it's fine because there's no rule prohibiting it. Rulebooks

or talk to the other players, if the game-rule-writers don't care

game.)

First of all, it's not true that you must be able to fake injuries and
influence the ref to make it in professional soccer. Many players do
those things and get away with it. But it's not required to succeed,
by any means.

Second, faking injuries is clearly cheating. Cheating is not part of
the game. If people get away with cheating (any kind of cheating),
then the powers that be need to figure out some way to properly
enforce the rules (which could very hard to do sometimes).

More importantly, make deals in VTES is not cheating. Even if you
consider that table talk and dealing is not part of the game, how can
it be compared to cheating, really?

> Shame, cause I like a game for what it is, not necessarily
> for how some/many others decide to play it.

Fair enough, but then again, who gets to decide what the game is, and
what it's not?

Mind you, I'm totally in favor of the "stop talking, play the game"
approach. Because yeah, I agree that some players talk too much, and
feel like they need to get a favour from every time they threaten to
block you, or that they need to ask permission for every single action
their minions take. And I also hate that some players will try to
secure a table-split without even trying to actually play the game.

On the other hand, politics, manipulation and interaction are a
legitimate, interesting part of the game. It's an important part of
playing the game. Sometimes people use table talk to avoid playing the
game, which is obviously bad. It doesn't mean that table talk is bad
in itself.

I like the game for what it is, which includes table talk.

Abraço,

Yeah, I think Peter actually has the wrong impression here. If two
players are talking a lot and you are bored, you don't get to make a judge
force them to stop. Your boredom doesn't surpass their right to work out
their deal.

On the other hand, if two players are talking so much that the game is
likely to time out, then that violates play to win. If the game times
out (with nobody or only one person or maybe two people ousted), then you
cannot win. In this case, it is reasonable to ask a judge to intervene.
Of course the judge will have to use judgment to determine whether or not
excessive chatter is actually going to cause the table to time out and
cost everyone the opportunity to win.

Matt Morgan

> Yeah, I think Peter actually has the wrong impression here. If two

No, no. I think I have the right impression, in that what you state here
seems to be the case. Which strikes me as very bad for the game as a
whole.

Granted, in this instance, where you use the word "boredom" (which
certainly is an issue, but less of an issue than the rest of the issue)
referring to my argument, really, it isn't so much boredom as "an
inability to play the game while I wait for other people, who are
inordinately monopolizing the limited resource of time". Again, I have
no actual problem with people striking deals, as long as they do so in a
timely fashion. If they don't, it seems like you *should* be able to
call a judge and have them stop. But that doesn't seem to be the case.
As as long as they are dealing "in earnest", two people can spend as
long as they want brokering a deal while the rest of the players sit
around and do nothing.

> On the other hand, if two players are talking so much that the game is
> likely to time out, then that violates play to win. If the game times
> out (with nobody or only one person or maybe two people ousted), then you
> cannot win.

If someone already has 2 VPs, and they then spend the next hour debating
a table split deal with someone who is in a "lost" position, even if the
are talking so much that the game is going to time out, they are still
playing to win--the guy with 2.5VPs wins the game when it times out, and
the guy in the "lost" position is better off with the game having timed
out. And as long as they are dealing in earnest, it apparently doesn't
matter that they deal so long that time runs out.

See, again, I have no absolute problem with dealing and
negotiation--this is a multiplayer game, and that sort of thing is
inevitable. But it strikes me that there should be, at least a
theoretical, limit to the amount of time people can spend on this
particular activity, lest it sideline the actual "card game" part of the
game. But apparently, this is not the case. And as long as folks are
dealing "in earnest", they can spend all the time in the world, and the
want of the rest of the table to, ya know, actually play the game is
irrelevant.

Which strikes me as a problem.

Okay, but it seems to me that if you're looking at it from a PTW
perspective, talking the table into a timeout shouldn't occur very
often.

> Granted, in this instance, where you use the word "boredom" (which
> certainly is an issue, but less of an issue than the rest of the issue)

> As as long as they are dealing "in earnest", two people can spend as

Well, it's very subjective as to what is timely and what isn't. I mean,
either the deal gets made and the game gets completed in two hours (legal
and, IMO, timely) or discussion drags on forever and the table times out
(not as legal - not necessarily illegal, but at least an instance in which
a judge could ask players to speed things up). So with that in mind, any
time you think players are taking too long, you can call a judge to rule
as to whether or not the players are risking violating PTW by talking so
much. The judge will exercise judgement and play will continue one way or
the other. That seems like the solution you're looking for.

>> On the other hand, if two players are talking so much that the game is
>> likely to time out, then that violates play to win. If the game times
>> out (with nobody or only one person or maybe two people ousted), then you
>> cannot win.
>
> If someone already has 2 VPs, and they then spend the next hour debating
> a table split deal with someone who is in a "lost" position, even if the
> are talking so much that the game is going to time out, they are still
> playing to win--the guy with 2.5VPs wins the game when it times out, and
> the guy in the "lost" position is better off with the game having timed
> out. And as long as they are dealing in earnest, it apparently doesn't
> matter that they deal so long that time runs out.

What you're describing here is slow play to take advantage of the time
limit. That's illegal. As always, you'd need the judge to see things as
you do, but such illegal behavior should be corrected. I mean, you've got
to look at the motivation behind the deal. Is the guy with 2 VPs getting
something from it other than timing the table out for the win? If not,
then it can't be anything other than stalling. And the guy who only wants
half a VP? He's not even trying. Call a judge.

> See, again, I have no absolute problem with dealing and
> negotiation--this is a multiplayer game, and that sort of thing is
> inevitable. But it strikes me that there should be, at least a
> theoretical, limit to the amount of time people can spend on this
> particular activity, lest it sideline the actual "card game" part of the
> game. But apparently, this is not the case. And as long as folks are
> dealing "in earnest", they can spend all the time in the world, and the
> want of the rest of the table to, ya know, actually play the game is
> irrelevant.

But they can't really spend the whole two hours on a deal because that's
not playing to win. You can't win if nobody takes any turns. I
understand LSJ's reluctance to put a time limit on deal making. I have
played games in which there was a lot of dealing but the game still ended
on time and one player won. That's perfectly legal, even if more than an
hour was spent talking. There's no clear line to draw here other than
whether people trying to win the game. If they are, then there's no
problem.

> Which strikes me as a problem.

I think the problem comes up when players sort of forget about the time
limit and talk too much without really meaning to. Or when they probably
can't win and aren't going to get anywhere and spend too long grasping at
straws. Of course you've got the types who will try to cut a deal every
time any card is played. I think your best bet there is to encourage
other players to ignore that guy and remind them of the time limit and of
the fact that nobody wins if the table times out. If players have come to
the table to win, then they should consider this seriously. If they
haven't, then there's your real problem. It's just masked by all the
yaking.

Matt Morgan

I would propose the assumption that deal-making is inherent to
any multiplayer game that is prolonged and where all players
compete simultaneously. (Just so we don't compare with figure
skating, for example.)

Let me expand.

A sprint-style game, multiplayer or not, doesn't lend itself well
to dealmaking. Whenever the task of making a deal obviously
lowers your average result it becomes more profitable to just
utilize the game-mechanics as efficiently as possible.
Compare running 110 metres hurdles.

Now let us compare with running 3000 metres. Taking turns
at point position would on average be profitable to those
"players" who are able to sustain a high average speed but
are less skilled at sprinting those last 200 metres to goal.
For the same reason "players" with less overall stamina would
benefit from acting together (making deals) towards a temporary
goal of sabotaging any attempts at keeping a high average
sustained speed.

For this reason I find the comparision with poker somewhat
halting. I would argue that one hand of poker (in a tournament)
resembles one round of VTES. A sprint style multi player game.

I(magine if you had to switch tables between hands in poker, or,
conversely, imagine that the normal VTES tournament was played
best of seven rounds before reseating, kicking out a few players, and
just repeat in absurdum until you have five players left.)

Anyway, a round of VTES is comparable with a long distance running
competition. Deal making is inherent to that kind of multiplayer
competition as different styles of "playing" can be used to achieve a
goal to a much greater extent than when you need to finish best and
have all of ten seconds or so to reach that goal.

When you add teams to the concept of multiplayer games (compare
bicycling) deal making becomes even more obvious. VTES has added
an explicit banning of this style of deal making to the rules
(collusion),
probably because of the overly obvious benefits from this kind of deal
making.

The very need to regulate deal making does in itself become an
argument
in favour of the view that deal making is indeed inherent to any game
where
such rules are implemented.

My argument is therefore that any game where your average performance
is lessened by the absence of deals (which you participate in) does
indeed
have deal making as an inherent part.
You can play without ever making deals, but you will suffer from it in
the long run.

Sten Düring

On 24 jun, 15:48, StenDur...@gmail.com wrote:
> I believe you're mixing concepts and comparing apples with pears (if

It does in Dutch, so I know what you mean. However, I think you are
the one comparing the types of fruit. ;-)

You see, you compare VTES to long distance running. I'd say long
distance running is comparable to VTES *with deal making*, but not
VTES *always*.

Take your analogy and transfer it to long distance swimming. Does is
still work? No.
The reason "deal making" in long distance running exists, is because
runners are not forced to stay in their lane, like they are in long
distance swimming. Instead, they are forced to get the best out of
being in a group and will do the things you say.
Swimming doesn't have that. Here, the athlete who actually is the
fastest (e.g. can cover the distance in the lowest time) wins. Not the
one who is the smartest in blocking/slowing down/using his elbows/etc,
but the one who actually is best at the physical action that is the
essence of the sport.

Let me put it like this.

In VTES, you can build your own deck. You can also decide how to use
your cards, abilities etc. as you choose. Meaning, in this analogy:

VTES = Swimming
deckbuiling = strength and stamina (= what you have)
playing the cards = going as fast as you can while not overexhausting
yourself, being able to "build up" your race, etc (= what you do with
what you have)

Let's say we could express the combination of deckbuilding quality and
card-playing quality in a number, say X. I'd say that whoever has the
highest X should win. Just like in swimming, the guy with the best
combination of strength/stamina and ability to get an optimal
performance out of himself (again X) wins.

When "something" makes a person who does not have the highest X win
(barring sheer luck and environmental factors), I think it's not
inherent to the game. It's added by people, who at some point in time
agreed (spoken or unspoken) to add this "something". Deal making does
just that, so it's not inherent.

> I am supposed to transfer up at least one minion to play VTES. The
> rules does not force me to do that. I would still say that
> transferring
> up one minion is an inherent part of the game.

Nope. The influence phase is inherent to the game, because the rules
force you to have one. The *option* of using transfers is inherent to
the game in the same way. The way you choose to use that option
though, is up to you (just like the option to play bleed bounce is
inherent to the game, wheter or not anyone uses it).

In theory, it should be possible to win without ever influencing out a
vampire, simply because cards that can do pool damage without
requiring a vampire exist. Extremely unlikely to happen, of course,
but the point is that a situation *could* occur where there's no need
for the use of transfers at all while still playing to win, so, again,
the option of using transfers in inherent to the game, but not the
using itself.

In the same line of thought, the *option of* deal making is provided
by the rules (because there's no rule that disallows it). Using that
option is a choice, however, and therefor not inherent. See again
"having the option to play while hanging upside down, or dressing all
in blue, because there's no rule against it".

> I am supposed to make (or break or sabotage) deals to play VTES.

Says who? Like I said already, it's perfectly doable to play VTES
without deals. You're only "supposed" to follow the rules and card
texts, and go through the phases of turns the way the rules say.
Anything else is added by *you* and not supposed to be supposed (heh)
by anyone.

> Mandatory and inherent are not comparable entities.
>

Indeed. That's why I formulated the title of this thread as a
question. :-)

> In no way is it mandatory for long distance runners to benefit from
> a tactical way of running. Still most everyone would consider the
> runner who took point for almost all of the distance covered to be
> either an idiot or a very inexperienced runner.

Or who has an insane amount of stamina but no sprint. Or someone who
is just that much stronger than all the others. You're not an idiot if
you refuse "deals" because you know you can win all by yourself. Was
Gebreselassi an idiot?

In reality the runners
> take turns at point position -- they make deals.
>

Sometimes. A lot. But not always.

> Only as long as all
> players agree upon suboptimal performance (no deals)

That's dumb. What are you basing the assumption on that play without
deals is sub-optimal?

And what is sub-optimal anyway?
Less fun? Not in my book.
Less challenging? Not at all, because deckbuilding and actual in-game
smarts become more valuable. You need to be real good with the cards,
not with your mouth.

> I would like to point out that agreeing to play in this suboptimal way
> is in itself a deal made.
>

It's the other way around. If you play a game with all the equipment
the game provides, using all the rules the game has, you're playing
the game. Allowing some, or all, players to add things to the game,
that is making a deal.

Teeka

On Jun 23, 2:40 pm, "Matthew T. Morgan" <farq...@io.com> wrote:
> Okay, but it seems to me that if you're looking at it from a PTW
> perspective, talking the table into a timeout shouldn't occur very
> often.

I agree that it shouldn't take the table into a timout in and of
itself very often, but the discussion that precipitated all of this
was about playing in an environment where dealmaking/negotiation is so
prevelant that it has the effect of scaring off/shutting out newer
players. Which is a problem in and of itself. And while it might not
end in game timeouts specifically due to people talking non stop for
45 minutes about a deal, it certainly helps to timeout tables that
would have otherwise been concluded normally.

There are a lot of ways in which one can justify curtailing excessive
dealmaking (PTW, delay of game if one detects a lack of "earnestness",
etc.), but the problem I seem to have here is that, according to this
discussion, negotiation is apparently viewed as as much a part of the
game as drawing, playing, and tapping cards. But the significant
difference between the two is that while you can justifyably say
"dude, it shouldn't take 2 minutes to pick your strike card." without
question, you can't, apparently, say "dude, it shouldn't take 10
minutes to strike this deal", as striking that deal, as long as it is
done in earnest is playing the game.

I'd really just much rather live in a world where it was recognized
that negotiation was certainly part of VTES, and that as long as it is
kept in the realm of reason, is ok, but it was understood that it
needs to be kept within reason and not lead to the pace of the game
slowing to the point of regular timeouts. And the default
understanding was "dealmaking needs to be quick and timely to keep the
game flowing" rather than "dealmaking can go on as long as necessary,
as long as it isn't obviously a delaying tactic".

-Peter

D Bakija <pd...@lightlink.com> writes:
>On Jun 24, 5:37 am, James Coupe <j...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote:
>> I think you're missing something.
>
>Nah. I don't think I'm really missing anything. I just don't like the
>default assumption.

Since deal making is an acknowledged part of the game, you pretty much
have to assume that players are allowed to make deals. This, by
default, means that players have to discuss them.

Similarly, by default, the player staring at his hand and saying "Wait,
this is a tough decision" is likely to be given the time to decide which
of two actions he should take. Even though he could be stalling, just
like the deal makers could, in reality, be stalling.

>> So it is with deal making. At some point, it will simply stop mattering
>> that the players are deal making in earnest because the judge will feel
>> forced to make a choice re: slow play, stalling etc.
>
>Sure. But way before the judge gets called in, the game can still be
>stalled/slowed unecessarily due to arguably unecessary discussion as
>negotiation is playing the game,

If it's not slow play and not stalling and the players were actually
negotiating rather than, you know, doing illegal things, why was it
unnecessary?

You seem to be in a situation where you:
a) support players having the opportunity for deal making,
but
b) don't want to give players the time they need to make deals.

Say that you, me and a horrible Arika deck are on the table. You and I,
to play to win, might need to get rid of that Arika deck as it will
likely kill both of us next turn with unblockable actions. We're
willing to fight it out at 2 players, but we need to discuss who should
do what now, to make sure we can take her out. And we may need to stop
and think when I draw into two master cards that I can't easily play or
get rid of, instead of the cards we were hoping for.

If the default assumption is that we're not allowed any significant
discussion of a deal, how would you handle a situation where we're both
dead unless we co-operate?

Taking a more extreme example, what would you do in something like the
Nergal tournament (unranked, but following the same rules), where
essentially two or more players *have* to join up in order to defeat
Nergal? And where a Nergal+1 player alliance can be unspeakably awful,
so the other three players on the table might want to spend some time
convincing the other player not to help Nergal?

I'm not sure how we can square this circle. Players sometimes need to
negotiate, but you seem want the default assumption to be that any
significant negotiation is, in effect, cheating (slow play, stalling)
unless the players can prove otherwise.

>and telling folks to hurry up is
>unlikely to accomplish anything.

If the judge believes the deal making was legitimate and wasn't slow
play/stalling, he doesn't need to get them to hurry up.

If it was slow play/stalling, it would be perfectly reasonable for the
judge to try to re-adjust the table so that it's not affected by the
slow play. For example, he might give the table back five minutes.

> > players agree upon suboptimal performance (no deals)
>
> That's dumb. What are you basing the assumption on that play without
> deals is sub-optimal?

I am basing that assumption on ten years of documented tournament
play all over the world.
Deal makers perform better that players who never take part in deal
making at all. Observe that taking part includes sabotaging other
players' deals.

>
> And what is sub-optimal anyway?
> Less fun? Not in my book.
> Less challenging? Not at all, because deckbuilding and actual in-game
> smarts become more valuable. You need to be real good with the cards,
> not with your mouth.

Suboptimal from a winning the game point of view. Fun isn't part
of it. Challenging isn't part of it apart from the competitive game
indeed being more challenging to play if a player refuses to take
any part of deal making.

>
> > I would like to point out that agreeing to play in this suboptimal way
> > is in itself a deal made.
>
> It's the other way around. If you play a game with all the equipment
> the game provides, using all the rules the game has, you're playing
> the game. Allowing some, or all, players to add things to the game,
> that is making a deal.

No, allowing some, or all, players to detract from the game is making
a deal. What is possibly worse, the word "allowing" is too often
replaced
by "coercing", in which case we're in reality leaving the realm of
"inherent to the game or not" and entering the one of "breaking the
rules".
The reason for this is simple: The only way to prevent players from
making deals is by removing potential dealmakers to be from every
table of VTES they participate in -- that action is already handled by
the rules under the header: Collusion.

Sten Düring

I don't think it does. If I negotiate in earnest and within a timeframe
that is necessary for negotiations, and the impending time limit means that
I no longer have the time left to execute the plan (ie I can no longer,
because of the state of the game, win the table), then negotiating as best
I can for maximum VP's becomes the new metric for PTW. Its back to deal-

the barrier" from having a reasonable shot at a GW, to an unreasonable
shot, then there's no violation of PTW, that I see, just a minor shift in
what is being legally negotiated for...

The fact that you can influence the position of another player by
*playing the cards* (there I go again, will keep emphasising it) is
part of a multiplayer game like VTES, yes.

My point is, that in a game like VTES that interaction should always
be "all for self".

Meaning, if you rush cross-table, you should only do it because
there's a gain in it for you, because you're trying to win.
For example, you're rushing your grandpredator's weakend, but about to
be re-filled, vampire. Your predator is close to being ousted, so next
turn the vampire might kick your ass if you don't kill it now, while
it's down.

Deal making is *explicitly* trying to better the position of both
yourself *and at least one other person*, at the expense of one or
more others. The above example is not, because you're only trying to
put the game into a state that's better for *you*, which might or
might not help anyone else, or even work for that matter.

the guy with the best
> > combination of strength/stamina and ability to get an optimal
> > performance out of himself (again X) wins.

> will have the rest of the table coming down on it like a hammer of god
> if

> Again, deal making.
>

Nuh-uh. A deck that is so obviously powerful (in terms of firepower)
that it generates all-out table hate is not a good deck at all (and
won't have the highest value of my hypothetical number "X").
A good deck hides its power until it's too late, which is in turn a
product of good deckbuilding and good playing skills. See LSJ's
signature Sun Tzu quote.

Bleed bounce is an exception to rules inherent to the game
> which prevent you from bleeding anyone but your prey and preventing
> that from happening by means of blocking only.

Untrue. The rules state that card text takes precedence over any rule
in the rulebook. What this means in essence, is that card texts are a
sort of appendixes for the rulebook.
The rulebook could just as easily have stated something like, "only
the prey and predator can block an undirected action, unless they play
Eagle's Sight or decide to block using Anneke". Which would have made
no difference to how things work. I've already said this, what the
rules say and the cards do, that is everything inherent to the game.
The rest is added by people on their own account.

Everything else I wanted to say in response to your post has already
been said by Emiliano (so thanks, Emiliano!).

The deck challenge isn't about right or wrong. It is about taking a
lot of time on your actions. I certainly think that there are decks
that can monopolize the time and that can win while its opponents are
still setting up.

I would probably start with something like this:

http://www.thelasombra.com/decks/amv.htm

Updating to get down to the legal library limit, and using 4/5 Madness
Networks, and Millicent Smith, Puritan Vampire Hunter. Swap out the
more questionable votes for Reversal of Fortunes to get more turns and
to keep your cross table allies from taking inappropriate (any)
actions.

Alternately, if I wanted to pursue Zopf's challenge, I would tweak
this one:

http://www.thelasombra.com/decks/madam_guil.htm

to simply consider each action, of which there will always be quite a
few.

Even this one will slow the game to a crawl:

http://www.thelasombra.com/decks/ok_stop_dots.htm

and it can take a game when properly prepared.

If Zopf really desired to work towards his desired goal, he would
simply play Imbued poorly. I have played against the best Imbued
players, and they can take less time on a turn when placing half a
dozen cards and taking 10 actions than players with only 2 minions. I
have also played against the worst Imbued players, and it is
excruciating.

In any case, deck building cannot ever convince rational humans that
table talk, deals, and twenty-thirty minute discussions are good or
bad for the game. Only direct experience can do that.

Since it simply can't be said enough in this thread:

Play.The.Game.

No, I mean you don't. As evidenced by the line below. Other people at

you. There is a separate line of thought, and a separate way of
handling, the ability for players to screw up the table - that's why
things like Anarch Revolt have been errata-ed/MRP-ed. Subject to the
qualification that players who turn up solely to undermine the
tournament can be ejected -
http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/cc64bbd830f82de0
- I can turn up with a deck that causes massive, massive table hate by
screwing everything. (See also Gehenna decks and the Imbued early on.)

If you never get a turn, you're not getting the chance to play it. If
your predator/prey doesn't get a turn and you're a wall deck, you don't
get a chance to block them. If you're a PTO/Parity vote deck and
someone throws Fall of the Camarilla, you don't get a chance to call
your votes.

No innate right. The table is just batshit insane and you can't do
anything you expected to do.

>> See also: Madness Network and Reversal of Fortunes, where the player
>> excludes some cross-table people from having many turns.
>
>Hmm. Fair point. But this particular (arguably abusive/broken in and of
>itself) strategy does so at the speed of normal play, where dealmaking
>does so at the nebulous speed of "however long it takes to strike the
>deal I want to strike".

Sure, it's normal play for that player. But you have 20 minutes where
you don't get to play. (Assuming the stupid deck works as it's supposed
to.)

If the argument is that 20 minutes of deal making stops you playing the
game, 20 minutes of Reversal of Fortunes can do the same. Note that
this may be interspersed with deal-making and other shenanigans because
at least one other player is getting a turn, so there are likely to be
plenty of opportunities for those two players to fight it out a bit,
cycle cards, argue over actions, whatever.

For 20 minutes, however, you didn't get to play the game. Just like in
20 minutes of deal making.

If the issue is that you didn't get to play the game, you *still* didn't
get to play the game you wanted to play.

>As noted in the "20 combats" example, sometimes it takes a long time to
>play out a turn. And when warranted, that is fine

In a very complicated deal, 20 minutes is possibly going to be fine.

If the "deal making" is:

"Oh, go on, rescue me"
"No"
"Oh go on"
"No"
"I'll be your best friend"
"No"

then it won't be warranted, and the judge can step in to control the
slow play.

You are the judge. Player A and Player B are discussing a long
complicated deal. Are the players actually negotiating in earnest, or
are they just going round in circles? Are the players making headway,
or are they both just asserting their position and not budging? ("No,
*you* take the 2VP end of this deal." "No, you do it.") Are they, in
your opinion, just wasting time and playing to the time limit?

If you think they're doing badness like that, spank them. If they're
not, don't.

That is, as a judge, exercise your judgement to determine if the 20
minute deal-making is in earnest, and isn't slow play. Come to a
decision. If necessary, announce and enforce that decision and, if you
feel it really is necessary, add time to the table in the same way you'd
correct the game state on any table.

>Where if two players are
>debating a deal, as long as they are continuing to debate in earnest,
>the players at the table and the judge apparently have no ability to say
>"move it along".

Sure you do.

You, the judge, are in a position to determine if the negotiation is
slow-play, stalling, or earnest negotiation. Use your judgement to
determine into which one of those categories it falls. Or any other
relevant category - am I trying to talk Bob into a deal so that the
table times out so that Caroline can get the Table Win, because I'm
colluding with her? You'd rule on that. Rule on this.

There are many other situations where you can be deciding between Slow
Play and earnest play. Is my decision *really* that hard? Am I
*really* so screwed that I need to count through every card in my ash
heap to determine how many copies of <X> I have left in my deck?

But if I took five minutes to decide whether to SR a card, you'd be
quite happy to rule it Slow Play or Stalling (if appropriate) right?

Do the same here. Determine if the debate is in earnest and really
could have/should have taken that long. If, in your judgement, we could
have done all this in 2 minutes, and have just been going round in slow
play circles for the following 10 minutes, slap us for Slow Play. If
there's a language barrier (I'm a native Martian speaker, you're a
native Plutonian speaker, we're both talking in Venetian because that's
what the tournament is being held in), it might have taken a bit longer
- and your judgement can handle that.

Use your judgement to determine if the deal making really is in earnest.
It's possible that it is. It's possible that it isn't. Rule
appropriately based on your judgement.

what my best move is any more than I want to be engaged in a 15 minute
discussion as to how best to make a deal.

game" (i.e. earnestly spending a chunk of time figuring out your best
move, even if that takes 15 minutes of planning and checking while not
actually changing the game state) *are not* ok while other kinds of
"playing the game" (i.e. earnestly spending a chunk of time debating a
deal, even if that takes 15 minutes of talking while not actually
changing the game state) *are* ok.

doesn't regularly cause games to time out, do not inordinately
monopolize large chunks of time, and don't generally scare people away
from the game.

>>Do you propose that the head judge

> you've expressly set out to do things wrong for no reason other than
> some deluded sense of making a point.
>

Not at all. I'm making the point that, in a game with time limits, time
is a finite resource. Since VTES allows me to spend this resource to my
hearts content, so long as the time is mechanically required by my game
play, I'm simply going to leverage that for Game Wins in the same way
deal-makers leverage their position for Game Wins through negotiation, or
the same way any other finite resource is leveraged for an in-game
advantage.
I see it as an outstanding means of controlling the table, and a great
way to stymie all manner of different deck tactics, which are all built
assuming that they'll get some reasonable fraction of the game time, and
that the game will be about 12-15 turns long. When I'm at the table,
both of these assumptions will be wrong.
Ideally, they'll see less than eight turns, and the ymay feel rushed to
get things going, which will foster play errors. The better I do my job,
the less time they'll have. Even if I don't do that great a job, since
I'm building my deck to do more in each of my turns, even knocking just a
few turns off the total available time will play to my advantage. The
concept is scalable, in that sense.

Having games at which a player is playing to this tactic, though, are
going to be pretty tedious. In that sense, another point is that, in a
tournament setting with timed rounds, a policy which lets one person
spend time _this_ disproportionately is a broken policy, and I'd like to
see it improved in some way, to make timed tournaments more fair.

DZ
AW

There is not so much difference. It shouldn't take you 15 minutes at a
time to discuss stuff in a game of VTES. If it does, either you are an
idiot or you are wasting time. If you are wasting time, the judge will
be happy to make you hurry it up or get out of the tournament. If it
takes you two minutes at a time, you're probably doing okay. (Though it
shouldn't even take you two minutes at a time unless you *really* love
to make intricate deals.)

I can't think of an occasion where people have spent 15 minutes
discussing nonsense other than maybe in some kind of high-stakes
tournament finals. They shouldn't really do it there either, because it
is only advantageous to the top-seeded player for them to do so, but
people do get all uptight and talkative in finals sometimes.

I think Scott just doesn't want to pin down a specific number of minutes
in the tournament rules because that is not how the tournament rules
work. Tournament rules rely on judges' judgment of what is and is not
reasonable and appropriate.

Josh

for example, a single hunt action should never take 30 minutes to
complete.

But what if the hunt is blocked, several maneuvers are played,
followed by Form of Mist, re-blocked, more combat cards played, Earth-
Melded, the now-empty vampire has to re-hunt, player negotiates for
cross-table KRCG intercept, re-blocked, Aura Reading reveals another 3
Earth Melds so the blocker plays a bunch of combat cards to dig for
intercept and wakes because he really needs to kill this minion...?
Giving each player a reasonable amount of time to think about their
card plays could very well keep this situation going for a half-hour.
Should the players be called for slow play? No, they were playing in
earnest. We can contrive examples back and forth for days.

There cannot be a hard and fast rule for when a given play is taking
too long, because there are so many possible permutations to consider.

If you have 30 actions to take, half of which are going to be blocked
and have a more-complicated-than-hands-for-one combat involved, and it
takes 30 minutes to finish your turn even though you have not played
excessively slowly or stalled for time, that is fine and part of the
game. If it takes you 30 minutes to negotiate a similarly complex deal
on your turn, but you neither do so excessively slowly nor stall for
time, that is also fine and part of the game.

The amount of time taken is only relevant (and can only be relevant)
in the context of whether it's an excessive amount of time for a given
play. 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 1.5 hours, no amount of time is, in
itself automatically excessive, as excessive is an inherently relative
term, and one that requires the use of judgment. By a judge. (I prefer
the Warden).

Dealmaking "in earnest" cannot be excessive, because "in earnest"
implies that one is thinking/speaking/acting quickly towards a valid
goal.

Yes, I find it highly annoying when two or more people spend a lot of
game time dealing, and it can easily lead to timeouts. But timeouts
are not against the rules, and neither is annoying me. But I'm okay if
you want to pester Scott to remedy that second problem :P

In message <pdb6-2199E4.2...@news-server.stny.rr.com>, Peter D

Bakija <pd...@lightlink.com> writes:
>But all
>discussion so far has indicated that discussing a deal is "playing the
>game" and judges can't tell folks to hurry along, as as long as they are
>earnestly playing the game, they are playing the game.

As LSJ has pointed out when Kevin asked, the Slow Play rules are still
part of the game and still apply.

- Deciding what action to take next is part of the game, and part of
playing the game. But if you don't do it in a timely fashion,
you'll get moved on by the judge.
- Deciding whether to DI a power card is part of the game, and part of
playing the game. But if you don't do it in a timely fashion...
- Haggling - not proper huge deal-making - over the terms of who gets
what from a KRC is part of the game. But it still has to be
done in a timely fashion.

And so is deal-making. If players are deal-making excessively slowly,
then it will fall foul of the slow play rules. Deal making is not a
protected activity, any more than the rest of the game is protected. It
can take as long as it takes, but if the judge thinks you're playing
slowly (either Slow Play or Stalling) he can act to have you hurry up.

Nothing LSJ has said indicates otherwise. Lengthy deal-making is not
inherently slow play, but when it is slow play, you can hurry people
along.

If a player really does need a bit of time to make a complex decision,
and you believe that, you don't move them along. If the deal-making
really needs 15 minutes, and you as a judge believe that, you don't move
them along. If players are playing slowly, you move them along.

>Which shows a neophyte player I think. Which supports Tetragrammaton's

New players can get stomped on for all sorts of reasons.

For example, at a UK tournament a few years ago, one player turned up
playing a Guns + Blur deck. Fairly simple archetype. Bleed or block.
Fight. On one table, he got sat next to an Immortal Grapple deck, which
he'd never seen before. Ever. He had no way of doing much of anything.

The players next to him would not be expected to hold off on playing
Immortal Grapples, because they are part of the game and part of his
deck.

It seems odd that, for example, a political deck that was playing the
game would, somehow, attract ire for making a deal with another
political deck on the table, so that they can both pass votes rather
than cancelling each other out.

In both cases, the newbie is utterly hosed, though.

The "problem" of newbies is usually best solved, IME, by being
supportive and helpful, but still playing the game. Aside from the
first couple of games, or maybe a game where he's playing something
utterly new, you should still be playing to win. In early games, you
don't play aggressively because the newbie won't easily be able to cope
with that, and you'll miss all the useful things like being able to show
the newbie a situation that hasn't come up before. e.g. don't do the
tactically appropriate burn of a vampire in combat, send it to torpor so
you can explain torpor.

In fact, I've seen and played in tournaments where a newbie would be
*utterly* screwed by Silence of Death. Why? Because they want, need to
ask for advice. "I've never played against Salubri before. Does Obeah
have any nasty combat surprises I might need to plan for?" "What does
'Circle' mean?" "I think I should rush Anneke or Anson. Anyone have
any thoughts which one I should worry about more?"

Since no newbie will be able to have all of V:TES in his or her head, it
seems unhelpful to tell them "Well, you may turn up and get hosed by
something unusual which no-one on the table will warn you about."

Messages.Body:
In message <pdb6-6199D7.2...@news-server.stny.rr.com>, Peter D

Bakija <pd...@lightlink.com> writes:
>In article <$HMArrR4...@gratiano.zephyr.org.uk>,
> James Coupe <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote:
>
>> Players who turn up with the express intention of undermining the
>> tournament and the express intention of playing slowly as much as they
>> possibly can... they're not very sporting now, are they?
>
>So if you go into a tournament with the express intention of using
>significant deal making and negotiation as often as it helps you, which
>can take up a considerable amount of time if done correctly and to your
>advantage, they are not being sporting?

Since that player hasn't, apparently, come with the intention to play
slowly or undermine the tournament, that doesn't seem unsporting.

Similarly, a player who plays badly - because they're really bad with a
particular deck but just haven't realised it yet - isn't necessarily
unsporting. A player who turns up with the express intention of playing
badly in order to force the judge to make many tricky edge case
decisions about play-to-win might play in a very similar fashion but
would, pretty clearly, not be being sportsmanlike.

Let me try this very simply, since both you seem to want to read
anything anyone says as saying "Deal making cannot be touched in any
way, and in reality is actually evil."

1) If a player turns up with the intention of being a complete jerk,
that's unsportsmanlike.

2) Turning up with the express intention of "ruining" several rounds at
the NAC is being a jerk.

3) Taking an appropriate amount of time to negotiate deals when it's
good play for you is not being a jerk.

4) Deal making is not inherently jerky. Nor is it inherently unjerky.

5) When deal making, you can fall foul of not playing in a timely
fashion, just as much as in any other area of the game.

Note also that planning for lengthy deal-making is extremely hard
anyway. Planning to have some deal-making capability is really easy -
if you have cards that can be used to the benefit of others, that's
fine. Parity Shift, Anathema, KRC, Rumors of Gehenna, Con Boon - all
good. Kindred Spirits cross table? Fine. Bum's Rushing someone else's
vampires? Just dandy. Dropping your Pentex Subversion onto the Turbo
Arika when it's stalled temporarily? Absolutely.

However, forcing the table into a situation where you have to make
*lengthy* deals is extremely hard. For example, if you play in such a
fashion as to force the table into really complex situations, rather
than progressing your own game in what the judge feels is a sensible
fashion, you may find yourself on the wrong end of a Play To Win ruling
before you get anywhere near deal-making.

Turning up with an arsenal that will let you make deals when you need to
is no problem at all. But when you make those deals, you have to do so
in a fashion that is not slow play and not stalling. In some
situations, that may involve lengthy deal-making, but it's hugely hard
to plan for.

So someone calls the judge over and says "Look, they've been arguing
over a deal that accomplishes nothing for the last five minutes."

Obviously, if the judge isn't aware of the problem because they're on
the other side of the room, they can't do much to help.

>> Player suggests a crappy deal that "accomplishes nothing at all" and
>> proceeds to attempt to negotiate it by going "nowhere" for 15 minutes?
>> How on earth do you believe that that's earnest deal making?
>
>It wasn't a crappy deal. It was a mutually beneficial deal that, after
>enough scrutiny, seemed to be more beneficial to you than it was to me.
>So I decided against making it. All of which was discovered through
>earnest, lengthy discussion.

You expressly said that the deal "accomplishes nothing". If the deal is
actually a good deal, that's different. But deals that accomplish
nothing are crappy by definition.

However, moving from a situation where you expressly state that the deal
accomplishes nothing to a situation where the deal is mutually
beneficial to make a point... that fundamentally doesn't work if you
want to discuss points.

Negotiating for 15 minutes over a deal that accomplishes nothing and
goes nowhere is not timely play. Negotiating for 15 minutes over a
mutually beneficial deal is possibly timely play (or possibly not).

Moot. You can call the judge in any event. The judge will use his
judgment to determine whether the player is playing slowly.

It doesn't matter whether the time taken is 15 minutes or 15 seconds -
slow play is slow play, and timely play is timely play.

If any part of the game is complex enough that taking 15 minutes to
resolve it is reasonable, it's timely play to take 15 minutes
resolving it. If any part of the game is simple enough that 15 seconds
is an excessive amount of time to devote to it, 15 seconds is slow
play.

>But David is simply suggesting building a deck that maximizes the use of

>same thing with no intention at all of undermining anything, just
>exploiting the rules to his advantage (which is what deal making is,
>really)? Again, how is this unsporting?

His motives are being a jerk, and maximising the amount of time he uses
in the process. These are not sporting. The act of deliberately being
a jerk is not sporting.

If another player turned up with such a deck and wanted to play it
without being a jerk, there would be a number of things that might be
doable. For example, if I knew that my plan was to make 30 Embraces
with 30 copies of Obfuscate and that this was going to slow down play a
lot, I might take steps to not be a jerk. Perhaps, if the judge okayed
it, I'd have someone else *not* involved in the game find the card for
me. With my back turned, I'd also ask them to cut the deck a few times.
This would reduce my excessive jerkiness.

If a player does object, or the judge does, fine, I play the deck
anyway. But I've made a concerted effort to not be a jerk. I could
still play absolutely by the book if someone made me, though.

There are other workarounds that could be applied in situations,
depending on what's going on.

This sort of problem comes from the same situation as players saying
"But LSJ! You won't tell us exactly what parts of a card we have to
read out when we play it! So I'm going to be a jerk and read out
everything, including noting where the smudges are, and who the artist
is and the copyright line and describe the set symbol in detail." That
is, it comes from people deliberately being jerks for no reason other
than the need to make some bizarre point that everyone already
understands anyway: in this case, things can take time, and people don't
like too much time being used. But we already have the solution:
judgement and sportsmanship.



satisfactory, the metric in particular is IMO very poor. Regardless of how

On Jun 27, 4:22 pm, atomweaver <atomwea...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> I'm confused, then, how this acceleration of _my_ legal use of the clock,
> due to your perception of "excessive jerkiness" is acceptable, but when
> Peter asks if its OK for a Judge to encourage deal-making to reach a
> conclusion because it is taking an equivalent amount time, he is told that
> the metric is "if the time use and conversation is necessary to the deal,
> it is playing the game, how much time is used is irrelevant." i.e. Don't
> interfere unless it is obviously stalling.

Obvious is unnecessary. Using judgment does not require that something
be obvious.

> If I accuse someone who is legally spending 45 minutes in bits and pieces
> across a round, talking different deals at different times of "being a
> jerk", do I get to apply unsportsmanlike conduct penalties, too? No, I do
> not. I asked LSJ if necessary-but-excessive deal talk could be limited
> under the Unsportsmanlike conduct section of the rules, and was told No, I
> couldn't. I asked if deal-talking that amounts to this extent (30-45
> minutes) of time use amounted to Slow Play, but since talking deals is part
> of playing the game, then No again, it is not Slow Play.

Taking an excessive amount of time to perform a necessary task is slow
play. Taking a lot of time on a task is not necessarily excessive.
Taking 30-45 minutes to deal is Slow Play if and only if 30-45 minutes
is an excessive amount of time for the deal(s) being discussed (i.e.,
we cannot without further information properly exercise judgment about
whether or not it is slow play).

But the assumption has always appeared to be that the 30-45 minutes
was being spent "earnestly," i.e., actively attempting to reach a
successful conclusion in a timely fashion. If it's timely, it's not
Slow Play. "Earnest" was probably a bad choice of words on Scott's
part, but here we are.

> So again, I'm left wondering why the double standard here, between deal-
> making use of the clock, and building a deck which makes use of the
> clock..?

There is no double standard. Actively attempting to stall for time is
against the rules. Actively attempting to undermine an event is also
against the rules.

> I've backed _every_ precedent LSJ has made up to this point 7 years in,
> with respect to using one's judgement as a judge, and shouted down a
> helluva lot of people here in the process. Because with his prior
> examples, there are game state factors that can be checked, player comments
> to account for, deck contents,etc etc. I don't have a single problem
> judging deal legality, play to win, or any other circumstance, up until
> this one of time usage. The "infinite, in earnest" time use metric is
> horrible, IMO.

Not infinite. Just not pre-limited. Use your judgment. 30-45 minutes
may be too much. It may not be. Without details, exercising judgment
is impossible.

> Here, the guidelines for judging leave an obviously big disparity in the
> way its applied, as evidenced by various observations in the thread. Josh
> Duffin _never_ sees deals taking more than a few minutes(to the point where
> he and you seem to take comments about 45 minutes of dealmaking as
> hyperbole), but Emiliano sees 30-45 minutes of a round spent deal-making
> with a frequency great enough to scare off newer players from the game.
> He was told that this level of time consumption is also supported by the
> time use precedent... which IMO, is absurd (or at least, bad for the game
> in general).

30-45 minutes is not excluded by the time use rules. No particular
amount of time use is. It is up to the judge to determine whether a
player is playing slow or not.

> I would think that this should make it glaringly obvious that time use
> guidelines with greater clarity are needed for more consistent enforcement,
> and so I asked for that; factors upon which to judge what is appropriate
> time use, and a metric against which to judge it. Neither are
> satisfactory, the metric in particular is IMO very poor. Regardless of how
> often you want to call me a jerk, James, there's some strong evidence that
> I just might also happen to be right about this.

Interesting. What's glaringly obvious to me is that this ruling is
exactly consistent with all previous rulings about using your
judgment.

Messages.Author: witness1



Ambiguity of meaning.

Earnest (from dictionary.com)
-adjective 1. serious in intention, purpose, or effort; sincerely
zealous: an earnest worker.
2. showing depth and sincerity of feeling: earnest words; an earnest
entreaty.
3. seriously important; demanding or receiving serious attention.
-noun 4. full seriousness, as of intention or purpose: to speak in
earnest.

Definition 1 seems fine for these purposes. If someone is serious in
their intention, purpose, and effort to play the game, then they are
likely not wasting time.

Definition 2, however, can lead to problems. One can be earnest (by
definition 2, showing depth and sincerity of feeling) in proposing the
same deal over and over again even though it is being constantly
rejected, which can reasonably be classified as slow play.

See also: http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/385ca09d54e3cff5

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <pdb6-247467.1...@news-server.stny.rr.com>, Peter D

Bakija <pd...@lightlink.com> writes:
>-If someone is mentally masturbating out loud on their turn, and helping
>other folks mentally masturbate with them in the name of striking a deal
>for an excessive amount of time, they can't be called on it for stalling
>(unless they are obviously stalling) and told to speed it up, as they
>are "playing the game".

This is simply wrong. You have been repeatedly told that this is not
the case. You are wrong. Repeating this sheer, utter nonsense is
wrong. I do not understand how you can have read what people have
written and then assert that they're telling you the exact opposite.

1) You do not have to penalise people for stalling. You can also
penalise them for slow play, which is a distinct penalty there
for distinct reasons. (Stalling is largely intentional, slow
play is largely not.)

2) Deal-making is not a protected activity. It is no different from any
other section of the game. If a player is not being timely in
*any* area of the game, you can move them along - be that
haggling over a vote, making a deal, making a choice of cards,
shuffling their deck after a Third Tradition, deciding whether
to prevent some damage or not, deciding whether to blow an Awe
now in the hope they pull a Voter Cap, and so on.

3) A player talking is not the same as a player earnestly making a deal.
If the judge believes that the players are not making the deal
in a timely fashion, using an appropriate amount of time, then
it *doesn't matter* that they're talking. They can apply
appropriate remedies and penalties, just as they can for EVERY
situation where too much time is used and players play too
slowly. It's *exactly the same*.

4) That a deal takes a long time is not proof that too much time is
being taken. But similarly, that a decision takes a long time
is not proof that too much time is being taken. Obviously, both
factors will be used in the judge's judgement! In *exactly the
same* way that you would look at a player's decision-making and
decide "Okay, you're taking too long. This is just silly now.",
you make *exactly* the same decision when deal-making takes too
long (or might have taken too long). You look at the situation,
you look at what's going on, you look to see what you think is
reasonable in your judgement, you look to see if the players are
being unreasonable in your judgement, and then you make a
decision.

5) A 5 minute fight over Rumors of Gehenna on this table might be too
long in your judgement. A 5 minute fight over a seat-switcher
(when they were allowed) might have been fine and dandy. A
minute to see how many Deflections have been played by your prey
might be sensible, but 45 seconds trying to decide whether to
play Taste of Vitae or not might be too long. You use your
judgement. Just like in every other slow play or stalling
decision you've ever made.

6) Deals are treated like *every other* part of the game. In any part
of the game, if the judge believes the play is timely, they
don't need to touch it. In any part of the game, if the judge
believes the play is not timely, they can apply slow play
rulings. In any part of the game, if the judge believes the
play is not timely and is deliberately not timely for an
external reason (such as deliberately timing out in order to get
a timeout VP, or to annoy a particular player), they might look
to apply stalling rulings.

Deals are not special. Within the realm of practical remedies, anything
you can do to affect any other part of the game when players are being
slow or stalling, you can apply to deals.
