In message <FzBgi.25893$y05....@tornado.fastwebnet.it>, Tetragrammaton

<nos...@none.com> writes:
>I do use judgement - i judge tournaments since seven years , so i have
>an idea of what it implies.

So could you tell us why you think that 45 minutes of arguing is timely?

>Peter atom and some other seem to have got the point - the question
>is not with the judge having to judge something special - if there
>are 3-4 players dealing, you *have* to let them the time needed
>to clear all of their arguments and counter-arguments.

No. This is wrong. You *have* to use your judgement. Everything else
is window dressing.

A player might, for example, introduce seven spurious arguments and
fifteen spurious counter-arguments for each one of them. Do you *have*
to let them do that? No, you don't. If you're letting them do that,
you're letting them down as a judge. You judge that they're spurious
and time-wasting, you tell the player so, they stop doing it (or you
eject them from the game).

If a player wants to enumerate all the steps that could occur as a
result, in infinite detail, as part of his argument, do you have to let
them do that? No, you don't. Step in as a judge and say "Billy-Bob, I
think Billy-Jean and Mary-Sue have got the idea now", and move on.

You *have* to use your judgement.

>then you *have* to lef that "part" of
>the game to be played.

You do. But it *must* be played in a timely manner.

If players are playing slowly, they fall foul of the general requirement
for timely play.

>And the idea of the judge having to step in a conversation in which the
>dealing
>players are involved for their best interest toward the GW sounds not too
>good
>to me.

You have to be able to do this. If intervening in the table when you
need to sounds "not too good" to you, you're judging wrong.

The deal may well be in the best interests of the players. If it's not,
you have other rules to apply. If the deal is in the best interests of
the players but the negotiation is *not* being conducted in a timely
fashion, you move in and correct the play. The players can still make
the deal, but you make them make it in a timely fashion. Apply
appropriate remedies, if necessary.

Example that might be an appropriate judgement: "You've all been talking
in circles for twenty minutes. Carol-Anne, Mikey-James and
Freddy-Kevin, you each have a minute to make your final proposal, and a
minute to come to a decision. I'm then going to add five minutes back
to the table. Carol-Anne, *looks at watch* go."

> A judge should be supposed to observe game state in general, not to
>be specifically the big brother listening all the time to *all* of the
>motivations the players
>may put in their effort to deal (earnestely), arguing and counter-arguing,
>giving and offering vps and the like.

No, the judge very often won't be able to listen in on everything. So
the judge gets the players to tell him what's gone on, with
disagreements from other players where appropriate, and exercises
judgement. It's imperfect, as any judgement will be, but it's what we
do.

If the judge can listen in the whole time - it's the final table, every
other has finished, whatever - then being "Big Brother" can be just
fine. Leave out the deals, I need to decide if Elly-May is playing
badly or playing intentionally badly to knock Jenny-Sue out of the
final. So I sit there, watch the intentions, and judge the play. Then
make a ruling. If this means I hear the deal-making too, then I'm going
to make judgements in the same way and correct slow play when I feel it
is slow play, and leave it alone when I feel it isn't slow play.

If you're not willing to intervene on slow play in a deal, seven years
experience or not, you're letting your players down. The deal can be in
the interests of the players, clearly. But if they're playing slowly,
you fix it. As you are required to do by the rules.

>
> There is no double standard. Actively attempting to stall for time is
> against the rules. Actively attempting to undermine an event is also
> against the rules.
>

Then you've set up a false parallel. I am attempting to do neither.

Try looking at it this way; deal-makers may spend what time they need to
negotiate a deal, so long as the discussion topics are pertinant to the
game at hand, and the conversation doesn't wander to not-necessary topics.
This can still lead to a significant use of the limited time avialable in
the round, which can have an impact on the availability of time that others
at the table to make their attempt at the Game Win.
All I'm proposing is that, since _any_ legitimate use of the limited time
available in the round is allowed, Time Use itself can become a legitimate
factor to consider, when choosing a Game Winning strategy. As with the
lengthy deal-maker who uses up the time available, I too can use that time,
so long as it is mechanistically needed. (I'm choosing this route, instead
of deal-making, because I'm frankly crappy at negotiating deals, I tend
towards brief, tit-for-tat, "I'll rescue your guy, if you don't bleed me
this turn"-type deals, and I tend not to trust my deal-partners when
dealing for extended returns).

So that's what I proposed. Among the Game Winning strategies I'm going
to consider for my next tournament, each will be gauged for its Time Use,
and selected on the basis of using more time, because that offers an in-
game advantage, and is legal. I got a lot of cries of "foul!"
"unsportsmanlike" "Bad play!" etc, in part my own fault because of the way
I presented this choice. That was somewhat deliberate, because I wanted
folks to see what the time use metric can do to the tournament scene.
I'm still going to bring a good deck, but its likely to be something more
like a Creation/Boon deck which uses Thaum to get the weenies Laptops via
MotS, and bleeds with Mirror Walks (maybe with supporting Cloaks from
whatever is Creating the weenies), than it is to be something which only
takes a more 'normal' number of actions per turn.
If it sounds to the Judge like it will result in a library which is
sufficiently random, I'll do two riffle shuffles, three or four overhand
shuffles, and a third riffle before presenting for a cut, and i shulffle
pretty fast; that'll be less than 30 seconds to do. Taken iteratively,
though, all of those actions, library searches, and shuffles will start to
add up. Will it add up to as much time as deal-making can consume?
Probably not even close. Consider the outcry to my proposed deck in these
threads in _that_ light for a minute; my best shot may not even come
_close_ to touching what Tetragammon is already coping with.

I might not succeed in chewing up as much of the clock as I might like,
but any un-balanced use of time which reduces the total number of rounds,
works to my advantage, if I build a deck suited toward that environment.

>> I've backed _every_ precedent LSJ has made up to this point 7 years
>> in,
>> with respect to using one's judgement as a judge, and shouted down a
>> helluva lot of people here in the process. Because with his prior
>> examples, there are game state factors that can be checked, player
>> comments to account for, deck contents,etc etc. I don't have a
>> single problem judging deal legality, play to win, or any other
>> circumstance, up until this one of time usage. The "infinite, in
>> earnest" time use metric is horrible, IMO.
>
> Not infinite. Just not pre-limited. Use your judgment. 30-45 minutes
> may be too much. It may not be. Without details, exercising judgment
> is impossible.
>

Its only the instances where 30-45 minutes is 'not too much' that concern
me, as Tetragammon has evidence that they detract from the game's ability
to attract new players.
Seperately, it strikes me as inherently unfair, in a tournament with timed
rounds, to have a legal means by which one player out of five can use as
much as half of the time available, or more, but those are the rules as
they stand.
The outcry to my suggestion that Time Use be a significant factor to
consider in building a deck may also be evidence that, on some level,
people recognize this. At some point, _each_ player should have an
opportunity to play.the.game. Somewhat unbalanced use of time is
reasonable, and to be expected, but the sort of legal time use allowed by
the rules as they stand is unreasonable. If one player's use of time is
impacting the ability of another to have enough time to _even attempt_ to
get the GW, something is wrong with the structure of the Time Use rules.
But, the rules allow this. As long as they do, I'll consider the impact of
this rule (like we do all others), when choosing a deck and a strategy to
Win.

DaveZ

No, but I found it particularly preposterous that multiple folks (Coupe
and LSJ) reacted specifically to what they believed my particularly
rediculous language to mean.

> Are you sure you know where the bounds of reason are, anymore?

Always.

> Scott
> has said - in the message you responded to - that dealmaking is required
> to conform to the bounds of reason, as determined by the judge, just
> like all other activities in a game of VTES must conform to the bounds
> of reason.

Here is one of the big flaws in all of this--everyone keeps pointing out
that dealmaking is treated just like every other aspect of the game, in
terms of use of time, etc. But deal making *isn't* just like every other
aspect of the game. Every other aspect of the game is bounded in by
rules, mechanisms and structures. Deal making/table talk is not. Making
it a very different animal.

When someone is tapping cards, shuffling their deck, or deciding which
strike card to play, I know, due to the existence of rules and
mechanisms governing these things, how long they should take, more or
less. I know that if some guy spends 30 seconds shuffling his deck, that
is totally reasonable, but if he spends 5 minutes shuffling his deck, he
is wasting time. I know if someone spends 10 seconds choosing a strike
card, that is reasonable, but if he spends 5 minutes deciding which
strike card to use, he is just wasting time. Due to the existence of a
structure that governs how these things happen. Dealmaking has no such
structure built in that gives onlookers or judges or the people involved
a meter to determine if a fair amount of time is being used or if an
unfair amount of time is being used. How long does it take to make a
complicated table split deal? 2 minutes? 5? 15? I don't know. As a
result, I can't judge if it has gone on too long or not (even if in
complete earnestness--the assumption here, which I'm sure many disagree
with, is that even an earnest use of time can be too long), like I could
if someone was spending too long deciding what their best move is or
shuffling their deck or choosing a strike card.

All I want, really, is for the judge to have the ability to get called
over when some player at a table thinks things have gone on too long,
and the judge can say "ok, move it along, this is a timed game...", even
if the discussion going on is in earnest. In effect, giving the judge
the ability to limit excessive time spent dealmaking, just like the
judge can limit excessive time spent thinking or shuffling or deciding
what strike card to play.

> or that the VEKN rules support what you're writing, either.

I don't think they do. Which is why I think there is a problem.

> If she sees it as absurd, then how is she doing it in earnest?
> Conversely, if she is in earnest, then it's not absurd to her, is it?

If I see it as absurd, I can get up and walk away and stop having my
time wasted. Karen Finley isn't holding me captive (mind you, I'm very
fond of Karen Finley). I can't so much get up and walk away from a game
of VTES given the same situation (assuming I care how I do in the game).



I'm judging a table. In that table, 2 or 3 players are arguing, trying

that this has gone on for too long, based on my personal judgment. So,
please, you have one minute to close matters and resume playing cards.

of LSJ's post made me believe otherwise.

strictly required. But "required" is also partly determined by
judgment. Even if the players are playing by the rules, it might be
required that you interfere somehow, maybe because of things you
observed. It's also judgment.

I'm sure that objective criteria would be used everytime, if it was
possible at all *and* if it was better than trusting the judges to
judge what's best in every specific situation. But that's not the case
here, I'm afraid.

Here you are plain wrong.

The rule says:
1. you need to play for a Game Win
2. Failing to get a game win, you should try to maximise your VPs.

So the one who takes the winning end of the deal is playing to win if
he gets a game win. no problem there.
The one who lets him win should get more VPs by making that deal than
by just playing. Again, no exceptions here.

Keeping a deal where you roll over when you already have a GW, isn't
against playing to win, because you already have a game win. Note that
the PTW rule doesn't care if you GW is a 2VP game win or a 5 VP game
win. It just says: play for the Game win. You don't need to get a Game
Win AND maximise your VPs.

If your final objective is to transition players of this newbie-
sanctioned format into the full-blown deal-talking mode of your base
group, SoD strikes me as a not-so-good-idea, because you want the newbies
to _learn_ about deal-making. One way to do that is to have them learn
it with a limited scope to the deals, so it doesn't overwhelm them
learning the game's mechanics.
For a start, just disallow table-split or lengthy partnership deals,
where most of the gabbing gets longwinded. Tit-for-tat, and one-round
duration deals are fine with most newbies. Or, you could say "all deals
are off after they have been in effect for one full round of play"
similar to what we do calling off all deals, once the tourney gets down
to two players. Or, just send them to game with Peter or me ;-)

I don't know that a newbie-sanctioned format will ever be practical,
because the population of new players is at most times very small. A
player either learns, or leaves, and for those who stay, I can only ever
see them playing two or three newbie-sanctioned tournaments before
they'll get the hang of things, and want to play in the big leagues...

Unions Versus Capitalists: The Eternal Struggle? :-)

I'm not sure that that is something not right. VTES as a multiplayer
game is affected by bargaining (or to put it another way, multiplayer
dynamics) in a way that most CCGs (being two-sided games) are not.
That's where a lot of the depth in VTES comes from. I don't see how
it's even possible (and I'm not sure it would be desirable) for VTES *as
a game* to address Emiliano's problem, which as I understand it is
really *not* that people are always taking a long time dealing, but that
people are dealing *at all*, which apparently intimidates the new
players who, he says, are having a hard time even learning the mechanics
of the game.

I mean, I can sympathize with that problem, but I don't think you can
*solve* it without making VTES into something that is not VTES. A
Collectible Solitaire Game, perhaps. Or Silence of Death, which is fine
as far as it goes, but clearly is not the VTES that we know and love.
(Its restriction against talking is so unusual that the only card game I
know of having a similar one is bridge, which is played in teams, unlike
VTES.)

Other than that, it seems to me like getting used to the mechanics of
the game in casual games before trying to play in tournaments is about
the best thing new players could do. I haven't really had the
experience of seeing new players feeling overwhelmed by the mechanics of
VTES or unable to participate in multiplayer dynamics, so maybe I lack
understanding here.

Josh

In my example, I implied that the dealing was stalled (and therefore
taking too long), a judgment possible to make based on table state and
the player's talking. Turns out that in this case it is possible to
tell them to get the deal done (or not) and move on.

I chose this example on purpose, because I suspected it was inside the
"gray area" of the disagreements in these threads. The questions are:
(1) Is a judge allowed to interfere with dealmaking if he judges it to
be excessive (even if no player called him)? and (2) What are the
(possible) guidelines for a judge to determine excessive table talk?

The answer to (1) is yes, and I think (2) is worth exploring so we
judges feel more comfortable about it. I have no problems ruling on
table talk if it's needed, but I would hate to find out that I
interfered too much in a given situation.

6.3.2. The Referendum

If a political action is successful, the referendum is called.

Some cards from older sets use the phrase "during a political action"
to refer to the referendum part of the political action.

The referendum consists of three steps: setting the terms, polling
(casting votes) and resolving the referendum.

1. Choose the terms, if any, of the referendum. Cards that are used
"during a political action" but "before votes are cast" are used at
this time.
2. Polling. All Methuselahs may now cast any votes they have (see
below) at this time, in any order. They call out their votes freely,
and there is no obligation to vote. Once a vote has been cast,
however, it cannot be changed. The polling stage is completed only
when all Methuselahs are finished voting (if you need a time limit,
the players can agree to wait 15 seconds after the last vote cast to
close the polling stage).
3. Resolve the referendum. If there are more votes for the
referendum than against, the referendum passes, and the effects of the
successful referendum take place. Otherwise, the referendum fails and
has no effect. Tied referendums fail.

Perhaps this could be stretched to table poliitics?
